extracted.intended_audience: health journalists, science communicators, press-release writers, and critical consumers of health news
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating health- and medicine-related news stories and related press releases, using the HealthNewsReview.org ten-criterion framework (with release-specific modifications). Useful for readers, reporters, and PR authors who want to assess completeness and accuracy of coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story adequately discuss the costs of the intervention?
rubrics_metrics.description: Our review criterion asking whether the news story addresses the cost of the intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Our long-term experience with thousands of stories shows that the cost criterion gets the most unsatisfactory scores. News stories don’t help patients and consumers if they don’t tackle costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story adequately quantify the benefits of the intervention?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story quantify how effective the intervention is?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New healthcare treatments should work well. When reading a story, people want to know: How effective is the intervention? Do the numbers back it up?

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story adequately explain/quantify the harms of the intervention?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story explain potential harms and their frequency?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the news, if you’re only hearing about the potential benefits of a test or treatment, run for the hills. What are the harms, and how often do they occur?

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story seem to grasp the quality of the evidence?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story convey how rigorous and reliable the evidence is for the intervention?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ideally, healthcare interventions are subjected to rigorous testing to prove they work. When reading about a new intervention, device or diagnostic tool, people should come away with a sense of how rigorous the evidence is for the intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story commit disease-mongering?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story exaggerate incidence or severity, or medicalize normal states to create demand for treatment?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes new conditions or diseases actually may just be opportunities to medicalize (and monetize) normal states of health. Readers aren’t well-served by stories that exaggerate or oversell conditions. Examples include turning risk factors into diseases (e.g., low bone mineral density becomes osteoporosis) or medicalization of normal states (aging, baldness, wrinkles, shyness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story use independent sources and identify conflicts of interest?
rubrics_metrics.description: Are potential conflicts of interest disclosed and are independent third-party experts used to contextualize claims?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Health care is rife with conflicts of interest. Readers deserve to know if the sources in the story have any conflicts of interest (for example, do researchers stand to benefit financially from the treatment they are promoting? Are they paid consultants for the company that manufactures a relevant pharmaceutical?). Readers also deserve to hear the opinion of objective, independent third-party experts, who are vital to backstopping exaggerated claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story compare the new approach with existing alternatives?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story situate the new drug/test/procedure among other available options and indicate relative advantages or disadvantages?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Just because something is “new” in health care doesn’t mean it’s better. When reading about a new drug, test, surgery, etc., readers should come away informed that there are other options on the table.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story establish the availability of the treatment/test/product/procedure?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story make clear whether and when the intervention will be available to the public?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New medical treatments often get lots of attention before they’re ever made available to the public. After reading a story about a new intervention, a person should be able to answer: Is it actually available to me?

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story establish the true novelty of the approach?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story explain what is genuinely new or different about the intervention (if anything)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often something that’s lauded as new or novel really isn’t. Or it may be new, but it’s not better. So, when reading about a “new” medical intervention, people deserve to know: What is truly new and different about this idea?

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the story appear to rely solely or largely on a news release?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the story disclose whether it is based primarily on a press release rather than independent reporting?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes news stories rely solely or largely on a PR news release–and never disclose that the information came from a news release. Readers deserve to know if a story includes no original reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: News release: Identify funding sources & disclose conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: For news releases, does the release disclose funding sources and conflicts of interest (editor's note recommended)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential conflicts of interests should be disclosed in an editor’s note included in the release. The funding for the project must also be disclosed along with any relationship that the investigators may have with that funder. Unlike news stories, news releases are not expected to feature comment from an objective expert.

rubrics_metrics.name: News release: Avoid unjustifiable, sensational language (including in researcher quotes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the news release avoid sensationalist, unjustified language that overstates findings or potential impact?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Red flags rise up in our eyes when we see terms such as: Breakthrough; could become the new standard of care; cure; first-of-its-kind; game-changer; Holy Grail; Magic; Miracle; simple blood test; this might/may/could lead to (which means, of course, that “might/may/could not” applies as well). Avoid such terms in the release and in quoted material.
